PPO's probability ratio and clipped surrogate on a worked mini-batch
RLHF: Bradley–Terry reward models and the KL-shaped reward
Direct preference optimisation (DPO), with a worked pair
intro.why: These are the methods used in practice today: PPO with GAE is the default deep RL algorithm, and the same machinery (or its simplifications DPO and GRPO) is how large language models are aligned with human preferences and trained to reason.
prereq: Session M11 (policy gradients, actor–critic, PPO clip)

sections.title: A2C, A3C and n-step returns
sections.plain: Run many environments at once so the training data aren't all from one correlated stream.
sections.body:
A single environment produces a highly correlated stream of data, poor for training networks. Instead of replay (which requires off-policy learning), run many environments in parallel:

  • A3C (asynchronous advantage actor–critic): several worker–learners, each with a local network copy, collect short rollouts, compute actor and critic gradients and apply them to shared parameters without waiting. Diverse, decorrelated experience; CPU-friendly.
  • A2C: the synchronous version: N environments each step T times under the same current policy; the NT transitions form one batch. Efficient on GPUs, easier to reproduce.

Both use n-step returns $G_{t:t+n} = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^n\hat v(S_{t+n})$ to form advantages $G_{t:t+n} - \hat v(S_t)$, plus an entropy bonus.

sections.title: Generalised advantage estimation
sections.plain: Blend one-step, two-step, … advantage estimates with geometrically decaying weights.
sections.body:
A one-step TD error leans heavily on one critic bootstrap (biased); a full Monte Carlo return is high-variance. GAE blends TD errors across horizons:

$$\hat A_t^{\text{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\gamma\lambda)^k\delta_{t+k},\qquad \delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)$$

λ = 0 gives $\delta_t$; λ = 1 gives $G_t - V(S_t)$ (ex1 verifies this numerically). λ ∈ (0, 1) trades bias against variance; PPO commonly uses γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95. Computed backwards in one pass: $\hat A_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda\hat A_{t+1}$.

Worked. $\delta_t = 1.0$, $\delta_{t+1} = -0.2$, $\delta_{t+2} = 0.5$, $\gamma\lambda = 0.8$: $\hat A_t = 1.0 + 0.8(-0.2) + 0.64(0.5) = 1.16$. A mildly negative next-step error does not erase a strong current signal.

sections.title: PPO's clipped surrogate objective
sections.plain: Reuse a fresh batch for several updates, but stop rewarding moves that change any action's probability by more than ε.
sections.body:
On-policy data are expensive, so we want several gradient steps per rollout. But after one step the policy has changed and the data no longer describe it. PPO freezes the rollout policy $\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}$, defines $r_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(A_t\mid S_t)/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(A_t\mid S_t)$ (a one-step importance ratio) and optimises

$$L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb E}_t\Big[\min\big(r_t\hat A_t,\ \text{clip}(r_t, 1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon)\hat A_t\big)\Big]$$

Clipping does not force ratios inside $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$; it removes the extra benefit of moving a favourable ratio too far, while keeping the penalty for harmful moves.

Worked mini-batch (ε = 0.2): (1.30, 2.0) → min(2.60, 2.40) = 2.40; (0.70, −1.0) → min(−0.70, −0.80) = −0.80; (1.30, 1.0) → min(1.30, 1.20) = 1.20; (0.80, −2.0) → −1.60. $L^{\text{CLIP}} = (2.40 - 0.80 + 1.20 - 1.60)/4 = 0.30$. Row 2 shows why the min must follow multiplication by Â: taking min(r, clip r) first would give −0.70.

The full PPO loss adds a value-function error term and an entropy bonus; training runs a few epochs of mini-batch SGD per rollout.

sections.title: A language model as a policy
sections.plain: Each generated token is an action; a whole response is an episode; its score is the reward.
sections.body:
$$\pi_\theta(y\mid x) = \prod_t\pi_\theta(y_t\mid x, y_{

State: prompt plus generated prefix. Action: next token. Episode: one completed response. Reward: a score or preference for the response, typically only at the end (sparse, delayed). Transitions are deterministic (append the token). This makes policy optimisation directly applicable to post-training large language models.

sections.title: RLHF: reward models and KL-shaped rewards
sections.plain: Learn a reward from human comparisons, then optimise against it while staying close to the original model.
sections.body:
Reward model. Humans compare responses; a model $r_\phi$ is trained with the Bradley–Terry model:

$$P(y_w \succ y_l\mid x) = \sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y_w) - r_\phi(x,y_l)\big),\qquad \mathcal L = -\log\sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y_w) - r_\phi(x,y_l)\big)$$

(ex2 recovers true qualities 0, 1, 2, −1 up to a shift from 2,000 noisy comparisons.)

PPO against the learned reward, anchored to the frozen supervised (SFT) reference policy with a shaped reward

$$\tilde r = r_\phi(x,y) - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$$

The KL term prevents reward hacking (exploiting reward-model errors) and preserves fluency. Watch out: don't replace PPO's old-policy denominator with the reference model. The old rollout policy controls batch reuse; the reference policy is a long-term behaviour anchor: two different roles.

sections.title: Direct preference optimisation
sections.plain: Skip the reward model and the RL loop: push up the preferred answer and push down the rejected one relative to the reference.
sections.body:
DPO uses the fact that the KL-regularised optimum has a closed form, $\pi^*(y\mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)e^{r(x,y)/\beta}$, so the reward can be written in terms of the policy. From fixed triples $(x, y_w, y_l)$, define the margin

$$m_\theta = \big[\log\pi_\theta(y_w) - \log\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w)\big] - \big[\log\pi_\theta(y_l) - \log\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l)\big],\qquad \mathcal L_{\text{DPO}} = -\log\sigma(\beta m_\theta)$$

Worked. Log-ratios +0.4 (winner) and −0.3 (loser): $m = 0.7$; with β = 1, σ(0.7) = 0.668 and the loss is −log 0.668 = 0.403. After training sharpens them to +0.8 and −0.5: $m = 1.3$, σ = 0.786, loss 0.241: the winner is more decisively preferred.

DPO is simple and stable (supervised-style training on a fixed dataset), but offline: it cannot explore beyond the responses in the data.

sections.title: GRPO and other preference methods
sections.plain: Score a group of sampled answers and compare each with the group average, with no critic network.
sections.body:
GRPO (group relative policy optimisation) drops the value model: for each prompt sample a group of G responses, score them, and use the group-normalised advantage

$$\hat A_i = \frac{r_i - \text{mean}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}{\text{std}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}$$

in a PPO-style clipped objective (usually with a KL penalty to the reference). It suits maths and code, where candidates can be auto-scored. Scores (1, 0, 0, 1) give advantages (1, −1, −1, 1); a group where all answers score the same gives no signal.

Variants of DPO: IPO (changes the objective to avoid over-fitting deterministic preferences), ORPO (removes the separate reference model by combining SFT with an odds-ratio penalty), SimPO (reference-free, length-normalised rewards with a margin). Each changes a different DPO assumption.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Reward hacking in RLHF: optimising a learned reward too hard yields verbose or sycophantic text; the KL penalty and reward-model ensembles mitigate it.
  • Value heads in PPO-RLHF are typically a scalar head on the same transformer, giving per-token values for GAE.
  • PPO's batch reuse is limited: after many epochs ratios drift and clipping makes most gradients zero; monitor the clip fraction and approximate KL.
  • Preference data quality (annotator agreement, coverage) often matters more than the choice between PPO and DPO.

code.title: GAE for several λ, and PPO's mini-batch objective
code.explain: Reproduces the worked GAE value 1.16, computes advantages for λ = 0, 0.5, 0.95, 1 on a short trajectory and checks λ = 1 equals Gₜ − V(Sₜ); then the worked PPO mini-batch (0.30) and what the wrong order of operations would give.
mistakes: Forgetting to bootstrap V(S_T) at a truncation.
Clipping the ratio before multiplying by the advantage.
code.notes: GAE is computed backwards in a single pass.
code.code:
"""Advantage estimation and PPO's clipped objective.

GAE: A_t = sum_k (gamma*lambda)^k delta_{t+k}; lambda = 0 gives the one-step TD error,
lambda = 1 gives the Monte Carlo advantage G_t - V(S_t).
"""
import numpy as np
def gae(rewards, values, gamma, lam):
    """values has one extra entry: V(S_T) (0 if terminal)."""
    deltas = [r + gamma * values[t + 1] - values[t] for t, r in enumerate(rewards)]
    adv, a = [], 0.0
    for d in reversed(deltas):
        a = d + gamma * lam * a; adv.append(a)
    return np.array(deltas), np.array(adv[::-1])

d = [1.0, -0.2, 0.5]
print("worked GAE (gamma*lambda = 0.8):", round(d[0] + 0.8 * d[1] + 0.8 ** 2 * d[2], 3))

R = [1, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1]; V = [0.8, 0.9, 1.1, 1.6, 0.4, 0.7, 0.0]
for lam in (0.0, 0.5, 0.95, 1.0):
    deltas, A = gae(R, V, 0.99, lam)
    print(f"lambda={lam:<4} advantages: {np.round(A, 3)}")
G = np.array([sum(0.99 ** k * r for k, r in enumerate(R[t:])) for t in range(len(R))])
print("check lambda=1 equals G_t - V(S_t):", np.round(G - np.array(V[:-1]), 3))

print("\nPPO minibatch, eps = 0.2")
batch = [(1.30, 2.0), (0.70, -1.0), (1.30, 1.0), (0.80, -2.0)]
terms = []
for r, A in batch:
    t = min(r * A, np.clip(r, 0.8, 1.2) * A); terms.append(t)
    print(f"  r={r:.2f} A={A:+.1f}: min({r * A:+.2f}, {np.clip(r, 0.8, 1.2) * A:+.2f}) = {t:+.2f}")
print("  L_CLIP =", round(np.mean(terms), 3))
wrong = np.mean([min(r, np.clip(r, 0.8, 1.2)) * A for r, A in batch])
print("  wrong order, min(r, clip(r)) * A:", round(wrong, 3), "- row 2 would give -0.70 instead of -0.80: the min must come after multiplying by A")

code.title: Preferences in miniature: Bradley–Terry, DPO, GRPO
code.explain: DPO worked losses (0.403, 0.241); a Bradley–Terry reward model fitted to 2,000 simulated comparisons; DPO training of a 4-response softmax policy from a reference; GRPO advantages for a group of four scored answers.
mistakes: Treating the reference and old policy as the same thing.
Forgetting that DPO needs π_ref's log-probabilities.
code.notes: DPO raises the best response's probability from 0.2 to about 0.49 while the KL to the reference stays modest (~0.29).
code.code:
"""Preference-based fine-tuning in miniature: Bradley-Terry reward model, DPO loss, GRPO advantages.

A toy 'language model' chooses among 4 candidate responses to one prompt. A frozen reference
policy gives log-probabilities; humans preferred responses in pairs (winner, loser).
"""
import numpy as np
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# 1) DPO worked pair
for w, l in ((0.4, -0.3), (0.8, -0.5)):
    m = w - l; print(f"DPO: log-ratio winner {w:+.1f}, loser {l:+.1f} -> margin {m:.1f}, sigma {sig(m):.3f}, loss {-np.log(sig(m)):.3f}")

# 2) Bradley-Terry reward model from pairwise preferences (true quality q)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); q = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, -1.0])
pairs = []
for _ in range(2000):
    i, j = rng.choice(4, 2, replace=False)
    pairs.append((i, j) if rng.random() < sig(q[i] - q[j]) else (j, i))
r = np.zeros(4)
for _ in range(300):
    g = np.zeros(4)
    for wi, li in pairs:
        p = sig(r[wi] - r[li]); g[wi] += 1 - p; g[li] -= 1 - p
    r += 0.5 * g / len(pairs)
print("\nBradley-Terry rewards (centred):", np.round(r - r.mean(), 2), " true (centred):", q - q.mean())

# 3) DPO training of a softmax policy directly on the preference pairs
ref = np.log(np.array([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])); th = ref.copy(); beta = 0.5
for _ in range(400):
    g = np.zeros(4)
    for wi, li in pairs[:500]:
        m = (th[wi] - ref[wi]) - (th[li] - ref[li])
        c = beta * (1 - sig(beta * m)); g[wi] += c; g[li] -= c
    th += 0.05 * g / 500
pi = np.exp(th) / np.exp(th).sum()
print("reference policy:", np.exp(ref).round(2), "-> DPO policy:", pi.round(2), "(response 2 is truly best)")
print("KL(pi || ref) =", round(float(np.sum(pi * (np.log(pi) - ref))), 3))

# 4) GRPO group-relative advantages: 4 sampled answers to one maths prompt, auto-scored
scores = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
print("\nGRPO advantages for scores", scores, "->", np.round((scores - scores.mean()) / scores.std(), 2))
